title: Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string made only of the characters `( ) [ ] { }`, decide whether it is valid: every opening bracket must be closed by the **same type** of bracket, and brackets must be closed in the correct order.

example.why: Every bracket is closed by its own kind, innermost first.

picture: Picture stacking plates. Each opening bracket is a plate put on top of the pile. A closing bracket may only take the **top** plate, and only if it is its partner: `)` takes `(`, `]` takes `[`. If the top plate is the wrong kind, or there is no plate at all, the string is broken. At the end the pile must be empty, because a plate left over was never closed.
idea: The bracket opened **last** must be the one closed **first**. That is exactly how a stack behaves: last in, first out.
See an opening bracket → push it. It waits on the stack for its partner.
See a closing bracket → it must match the **top** of the stack. If it does, pop. If it does not (or the stack is empty), the string is invalid.
At the end the stack must be empty — anything left was never closed.

say.1: LeetCode puts every answer inside a class named `Solution`. It is only a wrapper: the real work happens in the function below it.
say.2: The function we must write. It gets the text `s` of brackets and answers `True` or `False`.
say.3: An empty list used as a **stack**: we only ever add to, look at, or take from its end, which we call the top.
say.4: A dictionary that pairs each closing bracket with the opening bracket it must match.
say.6: Go through the brackets one at a time.
say.7: Is it an opening bracket? (The dictionary's *values* are the opening brackets.)
say.8: Yes: put it on top of the stack, where it waits for its partner.
say.9: Otherwise, is it a closing bracket? (The dictionary's *keys* are the closing ones.)
say.10: Is the stack empty, or is the top (`stack[-1]`, the last item) not the partner this bracket needs?
say.11: Then this closing bracket has nothing it can close: answer `False`.
say.12: The top is its partner: take it off the stack. That pair is closed.
say.14: Any other character is not a bracket at all: answer `False`.
say.16: Answer `True` only if the stack is now empty (`not stack`), which means every bracket was closed.

complexity.timeWhy: Each character is pushed and popped at most once.
complexity.spaceWhy: A string of only opening brackets puts every character on the stack.

steps.text: Our example: **`s = "([]{})"`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
We keep a **stack** of opening brackets that are still waiting to be closed. It starts empty.
This map tells us which opening bracket each closing bracket needs.
`(` is an **opening** bracket. Push it — it now waits on top of the stack for its partner.
`[` is an **opening** bracket. Push it — it now waits on top of the stack for its partner.
`]` is a **closing** bracket. It has to match the most recent unclosed opening bracket, which is the **top of the stack**: `[`.
The top is `[`, exactly what `]` needs. The pair is complete, so pop it.
`{` is an **opening** bracket. Push it — it now waits on top of the stack for its partner.
`}` is a **closing** bracket. It has to match the most recent unclosed opening bracket, which is the **top of the stack**: `{`.
The top is `{`, exactly what `}` needs. The pair is complete, so pop it.
`)` is a **closing** bracket. It has to match the most recent unclosed opening bracket, which is the **top of the stack**: `(`.
The top is `(`, exactly what `)` needs. The pair is complete, so pop it.
All characters are processed and the stack is **empty**: every opening bracket found its partner. Return **True**.
Done — the answer is **`True`**. Every bracket is closed by its own kind, innermost first.
